turn_text: I'm pleased to be with you. Thank you very much for the opportunity.

We have about 47 million Americans who are now qualified for the SNAP benefits, the nutritional program of the U.S. Department of Agriculture. In your view, is this program working to address hunger? And if it is or not, how should it be changed?

Well, quite frankly, first of all, it is about 47 million, about 22 million of them are children. But actually, the food stamp program is doing precisely and absolutely what it was intended to do. And honestly, it really is a program that increases the participation when you are in difficult economic times. And we are in very difficult economic times and have been over the last several years through the recession. It also then the participation decreases and it flows down when the economy gets better. And you will take a look at some of the indicators and we are beginning to anticipate that it will go down as the economy is better over the next few years.
Last year the House didn't consider a new farm bill or any changes in the nutrition program. As you look at the issue of hunger and the new farm bill, what are your biggest priorities?

Well, let me first say to you as an adjunct to the numbers that people who are utilizing the food stamp program, we're looking at nearly 50 million Americans today who struggle with hunger. And I've talked about the number of children involved. Hunger is a great cost to this nation. both in the abstract of lower test scores, per school performance. You've got about, if you do the cost involved in there, you're looking maybe about $160 billion a year in healthcare spending as a result of hunger. Let me just give you a fact from my congressional district. I represent the third district of Connecticut. Now, Connecticut, statistically, is viewed as the richest state in the nation. And that's because we have very, very high income people in Fairfield County. But it's regarded as the richest state in the nation. In my congressional district, one out of seven people are what they call, quote, food insecure. Now, that's just a very nice way of saying that people are hungry and people don't know where their next meal is coming from. So that has to be unacceptable in the United States. And that's where we are looking at the food stamp program. Now, what you're talking about is, and I'm just trying to get back to your question, which was on the farm bill. And what we need and it's through the farm bill, and that's the way we deal with a strong safety net, which is with regard to producers, but also to American family. And that is what is part of what the farm bill is about. And then if you go to American farmers, And you talk about their engagement with the food stamp program and nutrition and with food banks, et cetera. This is an avenue for them as well, you know, to help to address that issue. So that the Farm Bill has the safety net for farmers and producers. And it also is a safety net for American families in terms of hunger and nutrition.

I think that they're not struggling at the moment from the recession.

Congressman, let me move to the administration's negotiations right now on a trans-specific partnership. It would definitely affect agriculture. Have your concerns been addressed regarding potentially having this type of a trade relationship worldwide?

No, no, no. They have not. And particularly on the food safety, I had the opportunity, I think, twice this week. a once-to-with Secretary Bill Sack, and then yesterday, with Under Secretary Avalos, they came to testify before the Appropriations Committee, and I, at one time, chaired the Agricultural Appropriations Subcommittee, but I'm still a senior member of the committee, and they came up before us to talk about their budget request. My main concerns, as I expressed, were the the two pronged effort. One had to do with food safety and one had to do with transparency. And with food safety, the new procedures, which are being pushed by industry, present a really clear risk to the substance of our food safety standards, as well as the animal and plant health standards that are critical to the productivity of American agriculture. In November, last November, myself along with Representative Walter Jones and Senator Mary Landrieu, we wrote a letter to the Trade Representative highlighting our worries that we could see in the U.S. an influx of contaminated seafood from Vietnam and Malaysia because of the TPP, the Trans-Pacific Partnership, and in addition to which we would find that China may indeed use the Malaysia as a platform for being able to get into their products. And you know, I think that the number of citations or stopping at the border of contaminated products from Malaysia, from Vietnam, from China is in the hundreds. It's in the hundreds. So we ought to be very wary of this agreement as it affects our food safety and the public health of the people in this country. And what we shouldn't allow to have happen is that trade trumps public health.

turn_text: Mrs. Laurel, may I turn to one other area? And that is that you've expressed concern about antibiotics being used in animal agriculture. And I wonder if you would propose any changes in the way that this law is administered on the federal level.

Well, first of all, let me just say to you that antibiotics are an important part of medicine today. And I was pleased in March of last year when the federal judge ruled that the FDA must address the growing health threat that's caused by the misuse of antibiotics in farm animals. Now, I'm a longtime supporter of my colleague, Representative Louise Slaughter's legislation. that would phase out the non therapeutic use of antibiotics in livestock in order to be able to maintain the effectiveness of antibiotics in these animals. And so I think we need to protect the integrity of antibiotics and the same time protect the health of American families.
